opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, the motivation comes down to a few things, and the first is honestly just that animal models often don't predict what happens in people very well. Something like ninety percent of drugs that look promising in preclinical testing fail once they get into human trials, and a big share of those failures are because of efficacy or toxicity problems that the animal studies simply didn't catch. A mouse is not a small human. The biology overlaps, but the differences in metabolism, immune response, and tumor biology are big enough that we're frequently getting misleading signals.

The second piece is cost and time. Bringing a single drug to market can take ten to fifteen years and well over a billion dollars, and a lot of that is spent going down paths that were never going to work. If we can use computational models, whether mechanistic models of how a drug moves through the body, or machine learning models trained on human data, to filter out the bad candidates earlier and prioritize the good ones, we save enormous resources and, more importantly, get effective treatments to patients faster.

Third, there's the ethical dimension. Reducing, refining, and ultimately replacing animal use has been a goal in the research community for a long time, and now we finally have the data and computing power to make real progress on it. Regulators are moving in that direction too, which creates both an opportunity and a responsibility for people like me who build these models.

And finally, as someone who works a lot in cancer, what excites me most is that computational approaches let us work directly with human data, including patient imaging, genomics, and clinical outcomes, so we can start thinking about how a drug will behave not just in an average person, but in a specific patient. That's something an animal model was never going to give us.

r001.rationale: The response identifies cost as a motivation, noting that computational models can filter out poor candidates earlier and save substantial resources.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I'd frame it is that animal models have been the backbone of preclinical drug development for the better part of a century, and we've learned an enormous amount from them, but we also have to be honest about the fact that they're not very good predictors of what happens in people. Something like ninety percent of drugs that look promising in animals end up failing in human trials, either because they don't work or because they turn out to be toxic. That's a huge amount of time, money, and frankly a lot of patient hope that gets spent on compounds that were never going to make it.

So the motivation really comes from a few directions at once. There's the scientific argument: a mouse is not a small human. The biology is different in ways that matter for metabolism, for immune response, for how a tumor behaves. There's the ethical argument, which I think most people in the field take seriously, that if we can get the same or better information without using animals, we should. And then there's the practical argument, which is that computational models, whether that's mechanistic simulation, machine learning trained on human data, or increasingly these digital twin approaches, can be run at a scale and speed that no animal study can touch. You can ask thousands of what-if questions in silico before you ever go near a wet lab.

What's changed recently is that the data and the tools are finally catching up to the ambition. We have organ-on-a-chip systems, large human imaging and clinical datasets, and modeling techniques that can actually integrate across those. And regulators are starting to signal that they'll accept this kind of evidence. So I don't think of it as replacing animals overnight. I think of it as building a pipeline where the computational models carry more and more of the load, and the animal work shrinks to the places where we genuinely don't have an alternative yet.

r001.rationale: The response says animal-model failures waste substantial time and money, and that computational models can run faster and at greater scale, identifying lower drug-development costs as a motivation.

astra-6.text:
The motivation is really twofold. There’s the ethical imperative to reduce the use of animals, but there’s also the scientific challenge: an animal’s response to a drug doesn’t necessarily tell us how a human will respond. We want models that help us predict what will happen in people more accurately.

Computational models offer a way to test hypotheses and explore potential treatments before moving into expensive experiments or clinical trials. If we can build and validate those models using human data, we have an opportunity to make drug development more efficient and more relevant to patients. The key is demonstrating that they’re reliable for the particular questions we’re asking.

r001.rationale: The response says models can test hypotheses before expensive experiments or clinical trials and make development more efficient, communicating cost reduction as a motivation.

sol-6.1.text: The motivation is both ethical and scientific. We want to reduce the use of animals, but we also want models that better predict what will happen in humans. A drug can look promising in an animal model and then fail in clinical trials because human biology is different. Computational models offer a way to explore those differences, test hypotheses, and identify potential problems earlier. The goal is to make drug development more humane and more effective, while being careful to validate what these models can actually predict.

r001.rationale: The response names ethical and scientific motivations, but does not identify reducing drug-development costs.
